description: Hi, I'm Zach, an aspiring astrophysicist. I am dual degreeing in Entrepreneurship and Astronomy & Astrophysics at Indiana University Bloomington, but my home is in Dallas. I am familiar with astronomical data analysis using SAOImage DS9 and more, and am developing skills in Python libraries such as NumPy, Astropy, and others. I aspire one day to found my own research institute and make astrophysics a popular area of study. This is my first hackathon and I am looking for teammates. Please join!
summary: This website allows users to input celestial coordinates in either RA, DEC form or in degrees and view that patch of sky over time from data gathered from NASA's SPHEREx sky surveys. The website has five presets that users can use. The website includes many settings, including the field of view, whether or not to use GAIA data, adding/subtracting previous frames to see change over time, hiding incomplete frames, playback speed, and combining duplicate frames into visits. The output is a playback of the requested patch of sky and spectral data of any selected pixel, along with a zoomed out view of the first frame to add context. With this tool, any number of people can pitch in to spot oddities and movements in the heavens, using many pairs of eyes to do the work no human or computer can do alone.
details: Users can enter celestial coordinates or select predefined targets to retrieve astronomical observations across multiple infrared wavelength bands. The platform processes FITS files, converts observations into color-composite images, and displays them through an interactive viewer. Users can also explore spectral information, compare observations through flipbook visualizations, and overlay Gaia catalog data to examine astronomical sources. SPHEREx Sky Flipbook makes complex astronomical datasets more accessible by combining data retrieval, processing, and visualization into one interface. Its multiwavelength images help users examine how astronomical objects appear across different infrared bands, while its additional tools encourage further investigation. The project's goal is to lower technical barriers to astronomical exploration and encourage students, enthusiasts, and researchers to engage with publicly available space telescope data. The project was developed using Python, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Python libraries include Astropy for FITS processing, NumPy and SciPy for numerical operations, Astroquery for accessing astronomical archives, and Flask for the backend. GitHub was used for source-code management, and Render for deployment and hosting. Our project stands out by prioritizing accessibility and exploration rather than simply displaying requested images. We wanted anyone curious about the universe to have the tools to find and investigate unique observations without needing extensive programming experience. Throughout development, we considered scientific accuracy, processing time, usability, and the challenges of working with large astronomical datasets, while designing a platform that could eventually support additional data and analytical capabilities. While the premise is simple, tools like this allow humanity to explore the universe together, continuing a pursuit that has fascinated us for thousands of years.
